input_signals.name: Internal cash coverage of investment
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(TS_SUM(oancf, 3), TS_SUM(capx, 3)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms whose three-year operating cash flow comfortably covers three-year capital expenditure are funding investment out of proven earnings power, whereas firms investing far in excess of internal cash generation must lean on external capital and subsequently underperform.
input_signals.reasoning: This removes the raw, outlier-dominated GROWTH term and the internally inconsistent 2× multiplier: the denominator (cumulative capex) is non-negative and smoothed over three years, so the ratio is well behaved and monotone in cash-flow quality per dollar of investment. It is a single scale-free quantity in which investment and quality are inseparable — the same capex level maps to opposite signal values depending on internal cash generation — and it uses the sign convention consistently across shrinking and expanding firms.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( ts_sum( oancf, 3 ), ts_sum( capx, 3 ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Cash earnings coverage of capital spending
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(TS_SUM(ADD(ib, dp), 3), TS_SUM(capx, 3)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms whose three-year cash earnings comfortably exceed three-year capital expenditure are reinvesting out of proven earnings power, whereas firms spending well beyond internal cash generation are engaged in externally financed, low-quality expansion and subsequently underperform.
input_signals.reasoning: This is the direct coverage repair of the archive's best signal: `ib + dp` is the pre-cash-flow-statement measure of internal funds and is populated decades earlier than `oancf`, so the same funding-discipline mechanism should be estimated on a far larger and longer panel. The denominator (cumulative capex) is non-negative and smoothed, so the ratio is monotone in internal-funding quality per dollar of investment with no sign-flip pathology.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( ts_sum( add( ib, dp ), 3 ), ts_sum( capx, 3 ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Capital-productivity-weighted capex intensity
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(MUL(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(ppent, COALESCE(intan, 0)))), RATIO(capx, ppent)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: The same rate of capital spending is value-creating for firms that already generate high gross profit per dollar of invested capital and value-destroying for firms whose existing capital base is unproductive, so investment intensity should be signed and scaled by industry-relative capital productivity.
input_signals.reasoning: This abandons the acquisition channel entirely — no zero mass point, since capx/ppent is continuously distributed and the productivity leg is defined for essentially all operating firms — and instead measures quality as gross profit per unit of *accumulated investment* including capitalized intangibles, which is not a standard anomaly denominator. The multiplicative form is monotone-safe because the capex leg is non-negative: unproductive expanders sit far negative, productive expanders far positive, and firms that barely invest sit near zero regardless of productivity, which is exactly the economic ordering the mechanism implies.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( mul( ind_zscore( ratio( sub( sale, cogs ), add( ppent, coalesce( intan, 0 ) ) ) ), ratio( capx, ppent ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Accrual-adjusted internal funding of capex
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(TS_SUM(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, lct), che), 1)), 3), TS_SUM(capx, 3)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: What distinguishes disciplined from fragile investment is not reported earnings coverage of capex but *cash* coverage: firms whose investment is funded by earnings that actually converted to cash, rather than by earnings tied up in working capital, subsequently outperform.
input_signals.reasoning: This directly tests diagnosis (B) by reconstructing operating cash flow from long-panel balance-sheet items (cash earnings minus the change in non-cash working capital) so the accrual adjustment that separated the alpha-positive oancf version from the alpha-null ib+dp version is restored without the post-1988 coverage penalty. If the alpha returns at high coverage, the mechanism is confirmed as cash conversion quality of the investment program rather than mere earnings adequacy.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( ts_sum( sub( add( ib, dp ), delta( sub( sub( act, lct ), che ), 1 ) ), 3 ), ts_sum( capx, 3 ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Sloan-consistent cash funding of capex
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(TS_SUM(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1)), 3), TS_SUM(capx, 3)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Investment funded by cash that the business actually generated — earnings adjusted for the change in *non-debt* working capital — predicts higher returns than investment funded by accruals or by drawing on short-term credit.
input_signals.reasoning: This repairs the exact contamination the critic identified in the archive's best signal: the working-capital change now excludes cash (act − che) and excludes short-term debt (lct − dlc), so increasing the revolver no longer counts as improved cash coverage, which previously pushed credit-line users into the long leg. Because it is a one-term definitional correction to the current joint-evidence leader, any change in fmb and alpha is cleanly attributable to the debt-contamination channel.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( ts_sum( sub( add( ib, dp ), delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ) ), 3 ), ts_sum( capx, 3 ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Cash funding of total investment outlay
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(TS_SUM(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1)), 3), TS_SUM(ADD(capx, COALESCE(aqc, 0)), 3)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Funding discipline should be judged against the firm's *entire* expansion outlay, so adding acquisition spending to the denominator identifies serial acquirers whose internally generated cash falls far short of their total capital deployment.
input_signals.reasoning: This isolates a single design choice — breadth of the investment commitment — against Signal 1, and it places aqc inside a denominator dominated by capx, which avoids the degenerate zero-mass problem that made a standalone acquisition ratio uninformative. If alpha and fmb strengthen, the mechanism is about total capital deployment relative to cash generation rather than capex specifically.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( ts_sum( sub( add( ib, dp ), delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ) ), 3 ), ts_sum( add( capx, coalesce( aqc, 0 ) ), 3 ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Cash stock plus cash flow cover of capex
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(che, TS_SUM(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1)), 3)), TS_SUM(capx, 3)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Total internal resources available for investment are the existing cash pile plus recent cash generation, so measuring both against the three-year capital budget identifies firms whose expansion is fully self-insured versus firms whose spending depends on outside capital arriving on schedule.
input_signals.reasoning:
Removing lct from the denominator eliminates the collapse into a textbook cash-to-current-liabilities ratio the critic flagged: the denominator is now cumulative capex only, so the signal is a coverage measure of the investment program rather than a liquidity ratio. It differs from the accepted Signal 1 by exactly one term — the cash stock in the numerator — so it cleanly tests whether balance-sheet liquidity adds abnormal-return information beyond cash-conversion-adjusted flows.
REASONING_END
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( add( che, ts_sum( sub( add( ib, dp ), delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ) ), 3 ) ), ts_sum( capx, 3 ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Internal capital formation minus capacity expansion
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(DELTA(re, 1), at), RATIO(DELTA(ppegt, 1), at)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms that add more retained profit than gross productive capacity in a year are funding growth out of current earnings, while firms adding capacity faster than they retain earnings are drawing on outside capital and subsequently underperform.
input_signals.reasoning:
This replaces the retained-earnings *level* ratio — which the critic correctly identified as a cumulative-profitability and firm-age proxy with an explosive asset-light denominator — with a flow comparison in which both legs are scaled by total assets, so the measure is stable and cannot be driven by near-zero PP&E. The change in retained earnings is profit net of dividends, so the signal directly contrasts self-generated equity capital against the physical capacity being built with it, which is the funding-discipline mechanism expressed on the equity side rather than the cash-flow side.
REASONING_END
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( sub( ratio( delta( re, 1 ), at ), ratio( delta( ppegt, 1 ), at ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Improving funding adequacy of investment
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(TS_SUM(ADD(ib, dp), 3), TS_SUM(capx, 3)), 1), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm whose cash coverage of its capital budget is *improving* is transitioning from external dependence toward self-funding, and that transition is priced with a lag even after controlling for the level of coverage.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive has established the level effect but has never tested the change in funding adequacy, which is a distinct piece of information: firms can be poorly covered yet rapidly improving as capital budgets normalize or cash generation recovers. A change form is also naturally closer to zero-mean and less correlated with capital intensity, so it can add incremental content rather than restating the level ratio.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( delta( ratio( ts_sum( add( ib, dp ), 3 ), ts_sum( capx, 3 ) ), 1 ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Resource cover of peak investment run-rate
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(che, SUB(ADD(ib, dp), DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1))), TS_MAX(capx, 3)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Capital budgets are sticky at their recent peak — projects already begun must be finished — so the relevant test of funding adequacy is whether current cash and cash generation cover the firm's highest recent spending rate, not the amount it happened to spend this year.
input_signals.reasoning:
This is not a horizon re-parameterization: the denominator changes economic content from realized spending to *committed* spending capacity, so a firm that has just cut capex after a build-out is still scored against the obligation it created, which is precisely the fragile-expansion case the theme targets. TS_MAX over three years is strictly positive and far more stable than a single-year capex figure, so the ordering is monotone and the tails are populated by genuine over-committers rather than by firms with temporarily small denominators.
REASONING_END
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( add( che, sub( add( ib, dp ), delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ) ) ), ts_max( capx, 3 ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Same-period cover of capex and maturing debt
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(che, SUB(ADD(ib, dp), DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1))), ADD(capx, dlc)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm is genuinely self-funded only if its liquid resources and current cash generation cover both this year's capital spending and the debt it must repay or roll within the year; when they do not, investment is hostage to credit-market access.
input_signals.reasoning:
The unit mismatch the critic identified is removed — numerator and denominator are now both same-period quantities, so short-term debt carries its full economic weight instead of being scaled down by a three-year window. The economic claim is distinct from the archive leader: it says the binding constraint is total near-term cash calls (investment plus refinancing) rather than investment alone, and the denominator remains strictly positive and investment-inclusive rather than collapsing into a liability ratio.
REASONING_END
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( add( che, sub( add( ib, dp ), delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ) ) ), add( capx, dlc ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Replacement-adjusted investment rate
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(TS_SUM(capx, 3), TS_SUM(dp, 3)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Capital spending measured against the firm's own capital consumption identifies true expansion — spending far above depreciation means capacity is being added rather than maintained, and such expansion earns lower subsequent returns.
input_signals.reasoning:
This abandons the liquidity claim the critic found too close to the cash-holdings premium and instead normalizes investment by the accounting measure of how fast the existing asset base is being used up, which self-adjusts for industry capital intensity and asset life in a way that asset-scaled capex does not. Both cumulations are strictly positive so the ratio is monotone and well behaved, and it is a distinct economic statement from asset growth or CMA: it is expansion *relative to the firm's own replacement requirement*.
REASONING_END
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( ts_sum( capx, 3 ), ts_sum( dp, 3 ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Resource cover of capital employed
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(che, TS_SUM(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1)), 3)), ADD(ppent, invt)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: What matters is whether internal resources are large relative to the operating capital base they must sustain — fixed assets plus inventory — because a firm with thin resources against a large committed capital base cannot absorb a downturn without curtailing investment.
input_signals.reasoning:
This replaces the sign-unstable capex-plus-Δinventory denominator with a strictly positive stock of committed operating capital, so destocking firms can no longer flip the ratio's sign, and it retains the accrual-adjusted cash numerator that produced the family's best evidence. The test is substantive rather than cosmetic: it asks whether funding adequacy should be normalized by the *stock* of capital at risk rather than by the *flow* of new investment, which is the one normalization choice the archive has never varied.
REASONING_END
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( add( che, ts_sum( sub( add( ib, dp ), delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ) ), 3 ) ), add( ppent, invt ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Capital utilization versus own norm
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(sale, ADD(ppent, invt)), MA(RATIO(sale, ADD(ppent, invt)), 5)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms currently generating more sales per dollar of operating capital than their own five-year norm are running their asset base harder than usual, indicating that past investment is being absorbed by real demand; firms far below their own norm are carrying idle capacity that will be written down or left unearned.
input_signals.reasoning:
Differencing against the firm's own five-year average removes the industry capital-intensity loading that makes the raw turnover level a published DuPont/turnover predictor, so the surviving variation is a within-firm utilization state rather than a cross-sectional profitability characteristic. This directly targets the idle-capacity mechanism that produced a +2.6% alpha in the archive's gated version but with a monotone, non-multiplicative construction that should not invert the cross-sectional slope.
REASONING_END
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( sub( ratio( sale, add( ppent, invt ) ), ma( ratio( sale, add( ppent, invt ) ), 5 ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Flow-only cover of capex and maturing debt
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1)), ADD(capx, dlc)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Operating cash generation relative to near-term cash calls is the core mechanism, and the cash stock is a secondary buffer rather than the source of the abnormal return.
input_signals.reasoning: Removing `che` from the leader isolates how much of the 6.8% alpha comes from the balance-sheet buffer versus the income-statement flow, an attribution the archive cannot currently make because the two entered together. This matters economically: if the flow alone carries the result, the signal is about earnings quality servicing commitments (not spanned by cash-holdings effects), whereas if it collapses, the mechanism is closer to precautionary liquidity and should be developed on that axis.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( sub( add( ib, dp ), delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ) ), add( capx, dlc ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Unit-consistent smoothed cover of capex and maturing debt
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(che, MA(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1)), 3)), ADD(MA(capx, 3), dlc)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Funding adequacy is better measured against a normal-year capital budget than a single-year figure, because one-year capex is lumpy while the commitment it represents is persistent; smoothing both flow legs at annual-rate units should raise reliability without changing the economics.
input_signals.reasoning: This repairs the unit mismatch the critic identified in an earlier version — the debt stock is now compared with annual-rate averages rather than three-year cumulations, so `dlc` keeps its correct economic weight while capex lumpiness is smoothed away. If t-statistics rise relative to the single-year leader, measurement noise rather than economics limited the earlier construction, which would justify smoothing the whole family in the consolidation rounds.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( add( che, ma( sub( add( ib, dp ), delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ) ), 3 ) ), add( ma( capx, 3 ), dlc ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Persistence of self-funded investment
input_signals.expression: TS_SUM(INDICATOR(SUB(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1)), ADD(capx, dlc)), 0), 5)
input_signals.hypothesis: What distinguishes a disciplined investor is repeatedly covering its own capital program and maturing debt out of internally generated cash; the number of self-funded years in the last five measures a durable financing policy rather than a lucky year.
input_signals.reasoning: This tests persistence versus level within the winning mechanism, using the indicator as a per-year counter rather than as a cross-sectional mask — so unlike the earlier failed INDICATOR construction there is no degenerate zero-mass leg, since the count spreads firms across six ordered states populated in every month. It is also robust by construction to the magnitude outliers that force winsorization elsewhere in the family, which is the main remaining measurement weakness of the leaders.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ts_sum( indicator( sub( sub( add( ib, dp ), delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ) ), add( capx, dlc ) ), 0 ), 5 )

input_signals.name: Self-funding surplus scaled by firm size
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1)), ADD(capx, dlc)), at), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: What is priced is the absolute size of the cash surplus a firm generates after paying for its capital program and maturing debt, measured against firm size — a large surplus relative to the balance sheet is real free capacity, whereas a high proportional coverage ratio on a trivial capital budget is economically meaningless.
input_signals.reasoning:
Every archive signal in this family normalizes by commitments, which makes the measure explode for low-commitment firms and is exactly the pathology the critic identified elsewhere; normalizing the *surplus* by assets is a different economic statement — spare capacity per dollar of capital employed — and is bounded and well behaved for firms with negligible capex. This also resolves the tension between the strong-slope flow ratio and the strong-alpha stock-plus-flow ratio, because a difference scaled by assets has no heavy-tailed denominator at all.
REASONING_END
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( sub( sub( add( ib, dp ), delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ) ), add( capx, dlc ) ), at ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Short-term borrowing ramp per dollar of investment
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(dlc, 1), ADD(capx, dp)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms that fund their capital programs by ramping up short-term borrowings are financing long-lived assets with the most fragile liability available, creating a maturity mismatch that forces asset sales or curtailed investment when credit tightens, and their equity underperforms.
input_signals.reasoning:
This is a funding-*source* claim on the debt side rather than a rank blend of existing signals, and it is specifically about maturity mismatch — distinct from the equity-issuance anomaly and from the coverage levels, whose evidence comes from the level of resources rather than the composition of new financing. The denominator is the sum of two strictly positive investment quantities so the ratio is stable, and the archive's finding that near-term debt (`dlc`) rather than total debt drives the mechanism makes the change in exactly that item the natural next probe.
REASONING_END
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( delta( dlc, 1 ), add( capx, dp ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Worst-year funding adequacy
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(TS_MIN(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1)), ADD(capx, dlc)), 5), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Fragility is revealed by the worst year, not the average: a firm whose internal cash covered its capital program and maturing debt even in its weakest of the last five years has demonstrated a financing policy that survives stress, while a firm with good average coverage but a deep trough is one shock away from curtailment.
input_signals.reasoning:
This replaces the volatility construction the critic correctly diagnosed as an inverted commitment-intensity proxy with a stress-test statistic that keeps the same sign convention as every working signal in the family — higher is safer — so it cannot be an inverted version of the leaders. It is a genuinely new claim (lower-tail rather than central-tendency funding adequacy) and complements the accepted self-funding *frequency* count by measuring the depth rather than the number of shortfalls.
REASONING_END
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ts_min( ratio( sub( add( ib, dp ), delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ) ), add( capx, dlc ) ), 5 ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Weakest link of coverage and commitment burden
input_signals.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(che, SUB(ADD(ib, dp), DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1))), ADD(capx, dlc)), 1)), ZSCORE(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(capx, dlc), at), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm is safe only if it clears both hurdles — its resources cover its cash calls *and* those cash calls are modest relative to its balance sheet; failing either one is sufficient to expose equity holders to curtailment risk.
input_signals.reasoning:
This repairs the algebraic collapse the critic identified: MIN is not affine, so the commitment-intensity leg cannot cancel the coverage denominator, and the interaction is genuinely non-separable rather than a linear blend of cash profitability and investment. Both legs are standardized and monotone in the intended direction with no masked zero mass, and unlike the failed generation-0 MIN attempt the inputs are now the archive's strongest measures on a full-coverage panel rather than a thin post-1988 liquidity ratio.
REASONING_END
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( zscore( winsor( ratio( add( che, sub( add( ib, dp ), delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ) ) ), add( capx, dlc ) ), 1 ) ), zscore( neg( winsor( ratio( add( capx, dlc ), at ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Worst-year surplus per dollar of assets
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(TS_MIN(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1)), ADD(capx, dlc)), at), 5), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Durable financing discipline is best measured as the smallest post-commitment surplus per dollar of assets the firm has posted in five years: a firm whose worst year still left spare capacity has a resilient policy, while a firm with a deep worst-year deficit has demonstrated dependence on outside capital.
input_signals.reasoning: This repairs the two weaknesses the archive has identified in the durability idea — the six-state count produced coarse portfolios (alpha 1.6%) and the worst-year *ratio* version inherited the low-commitment explosion (alpha 2.4%) — by encoding stress resilience continuously on the asset-scaled surplus metric that carries the strongest cross-sectional slope. It tests the lower tail of the funding-adequacy distribution with the normalization that the archive shows is best behaved, so it should raise alpha well above the earlier durability attempts while preserving their FMB strength.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ts_min( ratio( sub( sub( add( ib, dp ), delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ) ), add( capx, dlc ) ), at ), 5 ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Internally funded share of commitments
input_signals.expression: RATIO(MIN(ADD(che, SUB(ADD(ib, dp), DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1))), ADD(capx, dlc)), ADD(capx, dlc))
input_signals.hypothesis: The economically meaningful quantity is the *fraction* of near-term cash calls a firm can meet from its own resources, which saturates at one: being covered twice over is no safer than being covered once, whereas every dollar of shortfall matters.
input_signals.reasoning:
This implements the concavity claim as a genuine capped transform rather than a winsorization parameter change: MIN caps the numerator at the commitment level, so the signal is bounded above at exactly 1.0 and continues to discriminate without limit on the deficit side, which is where the economics lives. Because the upper tail is eliminated by construction rather than trimmed, the low-capex firms that inflate the parent ratio can no longer occupy the extreme long leg, which should raise the cross-sectional slope while preserving the spread driven by shortfall firms.
REASONING_END
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ratio( min( add( che, sub( add( ib, dp ), delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ) ) ), add( capx, dlc ) ), add( capx, dlc ) )

input_signals.name: Trough cash generation cover of commitments
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(che, TS_MIN(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1)), 3)), ADD(capx, dlc)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Funding capacity should be judged on the cash generation a firm can rely on, proxied by its weakest of the last three years, because the latest year may be a cyclical peak that will not recur when the capital program still has to be paid for.
input_signals.reasoning:
This replaces the degenerate cross-measure MIN — where gross profit almost always dominates cash earnings and the operator never binds — with a MIN across time, which binds for every firm and encodes sustainable rather than latest funding capacity. It differs from the accepted worst-year surplus signal because commitments and the cash buffer are measured at current levels while only the recurring flow is taken at its trough, isolating durability of the earnings engine rather than of the entire surplus.
REASONING_END

input_signals.name: Financing discipline plus operating utilization
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(ADD(che, SUB(ADD(ib, dp), DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1))), ADD(capx, dlc)), SUB(RATIO(sale, ADD(ppent, invt)), MA(RATIO(sale, ADD(ppent, invt)), 5)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Productive investment requires both that the firm can pay for it and that the capital already in place is being worked harder than usual; financing adequacy and capacity utilization are separate conditions, and firms satisfying both are the disciplined investors the theme identifies.
input_signals.reasoning:
Unlike the rejected blend, the two legs share no variables and no numerator: one is a balance-sheet financing ratio, the other a within-firm operating-utilization deviation, so their correlation is low by construction. The pairing is also targeted at the archive's central tension — the utilization leg carries strong cross-sectional evidence with no alpha (fmb 3.57, alpha 0.1%) while the coverage leg carries strong alpha with a weaker slope — so combining independent legs should produce joint strength rather than reproduce either parent.
REASONING_END

input_signals.name: Funding adequacy plus investment restraint

input_signals.hypothesis: Disciplined investment requires both that the firm can pay for its capital program and that the program is modest relative to the capital it is actually consuming; a firm spending several times its depreciation is expanding aggressively even if it is currently well funded.
input_signals.reasoning: These two legs carry the archive's strongest alpha (7.1%) and strongest cross-sectional slope (fmb −4.37 in restraint form) respectively, and they are economically distinct — one is about the sources of cash, the other about the scale of expansion relative to capital consumption — so this is not a re-scaling of a single construct. input_signals.hypothesis: The three conditions are conjunctive rather than additive: a firm that fails badly on any one of funding adequacy, expansion restraint or capacity utilization is not a disciplined investor, and averaging ranks lets a strong leg mask a disqualifying weakness.
input_signals.reasoning: This tests aggregation *structure* against Signal 2 with identical economic content, which is the one remaining design question worth a slot: SUMRANK is a linear blend while MIN is a non-separable screen that only rewards firms clearing every hurdle. The earlier MIN attempts are informative here — the failed generation-0 version used thin post-1988 inputs, while the successful generation-6 version (alpha 4.9%, t=5.00) showed the operator works when the legs are well measured, so a three-way screen on the archive's best legs is a genuine test rather than a repeat.

input_signals.hypothesis: Once maturing debt is included in the commitment denominator, the working-capital adjustment to the numerator becomes economically redundant, because firms that inflate earnings through working capital also carry the short-term debt that funds it.
input_signals.reasoning: The accrual adjustment was decisive in the capex-only family (alpha 0.4% without it versus 4.1% with it), but that comparison predates the debt term and has never been rerun with the current denominator — and the simpler numerator lifts coverage from 0.110 toward 0.134 by removing the need for a prior-year balance-sheet reconstruction. If evidence is preserved, the family's best form is materially simpler and applies to a substantially larger panel, which matters for the reliability of the final recommendation.

input_signals.reasoning: The gross-profit coverage leg delivered 6.0% alpha at the family's highest coverage (0.134) but the weakest slope (fmb 1.52), and the utilization leg is precisely the slope-rich, alpha-poor complement, so pairing them targets the joint objective on the largest available panel. input_signals.expression: ADD(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(che, MA(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1)), 3)), ADD(MA(capx, 3), dlc)), 1)), ADD(ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(TS_SUM(capx, 3), TS_SUM(dp, 3))), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(sale, ADD(ppent, invt)), MA(RATIO(sale, ADD(ppent, invt)), 5)), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Funding adequacy, expansion restraint relative to capital consumption, and above-norm use of installed capital are three co-equal conditions for productive investment, and a firm's quality is the sum of its standing on all three measured on a common scale.
input_signals.reasoning:
The weighting defect the critic identified is fixed by explicit standardization and addition, which gives each channel exactly one third of the weight as the hypothesis requires, rather than the 50/25/25 split that nested SUMRANK imposes silently. The legs do reuse capx, dp, sale and invt in different roles — a coverage denominator, a consumption ratio and a turnover deviation — but their empirical profiles are close to orthogonal in the archive (alpha 7.1%/fmb 2.15, alpha 0.3%/fmb −4.37, alpha 0.1%/fmb 3.57), and paired with the accepted conjunctive screen this isolates whether additive or conjunctive aggregation of the same three channels serves the joint objective better.

input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(che, TS_SUM(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1)), 3)), ADD(TS_SUM(capx, 3), TS_SUM(dlc, 3))), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Funding adequacy is best measured over a full investment cycle: cash on hand plus three years of cash generation against three years of capital spending and three years of short-term debt obligations, so that neither lumpy capex nor a single year's refinancing schedule distorts the assessment.
input_signals.reasoning: This is the one combination the archive has never tested cleanly — three-year cumulation delivers the family's strongest slope and Sharpe (fmb 3.72, 0.41) while maturing debt delivers its strongest alpha (6.8–7.1%) — and it is dimensionally consistent because both denominator terms are three-year sums, repairing the unit error that made the earlier hybrid capex-dominated. If the two effects are additive rather than substitutes, this should be the archive's best joint-evidence signal.

input_signals.name: Cover of fixed, working-capital and debt cash calls
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(che, TS_SUM(ADD(ib, dp), 3)), ADD(ADD(TS_SUM(capx, 3), TS_SUM(dlc, 3)), DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 3))), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Over an investment cycle a firm's cash calls are threefold — fixed capital spending, the cash permanently sunk into growing working capital, and short-term debt to be repaid — and resources should be measured against all three rather than netting the working-capital build out of earnings.
input_signals.reasoning:
The critic's telescoping observation is exactly right and turns into a new economic claim rather than an ablation: the three-year working-capital change is a genuine, systematically growing investment outlay, so it belongs on the commitment side of the ledger where it competes with capex for the same cash, and DELTA(WC, 3) measures it directly at the same horizon as the other two terms. This is a substantively different accounting of investment from every archive signal — which treats working capital only as a deduction from cash generation — and the denominator remains dominated by the two strictly positive three-year sums, so the ordering stays stable.

input_signals.name: Self-funding surplus weighted by capital irreversibility
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(MUL(RATIO(ppegt, at), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1)), ADD(capx, dlc)), at), 1))), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Self-funding matters most where capital is irreversible: for a firm whose balance sheet is dominated by gross fixed assets, a funding shortfall forces distressed sales of assets that cannot be redeployed, whereas an asset-light firm can retrench cheaply, so the same surplus or deficit carries very different consequences.
input_signals.reasoning:
This is the theme's core interaction claim implemented without the defects of earlier attempts — the weighting variable (gross PP&E over assets) appears nowhere in the surplus measure, so nothing cancels algebraically as it did when commitment intensity multiplied a commitment-scaled ratio, and the weight is strictly non-negative and bounded in [0, 1], so the ordering is monotone in the surplus with no masked zero mass. It pairs the archive's best-slope funding measure (asset-scaled surplus, fmb 3.54, alpha 4.3%) with a real-options conditioning variable rather than a third numerator swap in an already twice-tested composite.
